lede: Where the sources speak about the same thing, their voices stand side by side.

pairs.frage: Was there an organized committee of killers at Sarasota in 1884?
pairs.note: A member testified to “the Sara Sota Vigilance Committee, styled S. S. V. C.”, its meetings and its members; a Jacksonville paper called it “a society of thugs”. A neighbour, speaking in Buffalo, denied that there was ever “any formal organization” and blamed “a number of bad, unscrupulous men”. The juries and the Supreme Court followed the testimony.

voices.wer: Thomas L. Dryman and Louis L. Cato, in court, 1885

pairs.frage: How did the colony fare in its first weeks?
pairs.note: The promoter wrote on 4 January 1886 that the colonists continued in excellent health and were settling on their lands “contented and hopeful”. Five days later, by a colonist's memoir, snow fell; a diary of the same weeks ends with “Start today for Tampa.”

pairs.frage: Who was responsible for the failure of the colony?
pairs.note: A London writer in 1887 blamed the promoter's plausibility, a board that had never seen Florida, and the choice of “elderly men and fathers of families”. The town's historian in 1946 called the directors “men of honor and integrity” and looked for the cause elsewhere.

pairs.frage: What did Sarasota promise about its winters, and what happened?
pairs.note: In 1884 an Edinburgh prospectus sold land on the bay as lying “below the frost line”; a colonist remembered the snow of January 1886. In about 1922 a county booklet promised a place “free from chilling frost dangers and discomforts”. The promise outlived the colony by forty years.

A booklet of about 1924 announced that the keys would become “the theater of the most ambitious and artistic landscape development ever attempted in Florida”. In February 1926 the causeway opened with concerts and free buses; the town historian of 1946 doubted the million dollars of sales reported for the first day.

pairs.frage: How did the law meet violence in the county's first year?
pairs.note: In January 1921 a mob gathered a rope for a white man suspected of killing a former mayor; the sheriff took him away and he was released for want of evidence. In June a white guard was bound over for the murder of a Black prisoner whom the paper does not name. What became of that case is not known.
